accuracy.evidence: Covers all three evidence statements of the topic: an example of feelings changing in one day (Pip's five-event day and the learner's own day), why two children feel differently about the same event (clue cards tied to desires and past experience, the factors Harris et al. 1989 and Pons, Harris and de Rosnay 2004 show 5-7 year olds start to use), and feelings being temporary (the cross cloud that passes). It never says any feeling is wrong, and it notes mixed feelings, which children understand later, as possible rather than required.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the beliefs children of this age commonly hold: a bad mood lasts all day (day prediction, challenge 'stuck', p1, m1); one event has one right feeling, so a friend who differs is wrong or silly (two-child prediction, 'Who has the wrong feeling? Nobody', m2, m3, m6, challenge 'wrong'/'fake'); telling someone to stop feeling sad (kind step, 'stopit'); only one feeling at a time (challenge 'two', m5); and hitting to get rid of anger (the cloud grows, 'hit', m4).

lab_distinct.evidence: Distinct from flagfeel, which builds faces by moving brows and mouth. Here the faces are fixed tokens dragged onto events: a five-slot day timeline that draws a rising and falling mood line, a two-child clue-card comparison where the same event takes two different faces, a storm cloud over Pip that shrinks with calm helpers and grows with hurtful ones, and a kind-reply chooser. The 6-token shingle gate passed against every flagship lab, including flagfeel and flagtry.

lab_teaches.evidence: Learners see the ideas instead of being told them: the mood line literally goes up and down as they fill Pip's day; the two-child step will not accept 'scared' for Mia or 'happy' for Leo, so the clue card, not the event, decides the feeling; dragging 'Hit my brother' onto Pip makes the cloud bigger while 'Hug my teddy' shrinks it; and in the sandbox the line for their own day shows how many times their feelings changed.

predictions.evidence: Four locked predictions, each followed by a task that answers it: will Pip feel happy all day (no: the line drops at breakfast), will Mia and Leo feel the same about the same dog (not always: the clues lead to happy and scared), how long a very cross feeling lasts (it passes as the cloud clears), and who has the wrong feeling (nobody, which the kind replies then put into words).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven challenge kinds (change, differ, kind, pass, help, why, two) rotate with shuffled answer order. Ten distinct feedback messages explain each wrong choice, for example 'Nobody is wrong. People feel different things because they are different', 'You can't switch off someone's feeling. Say that you see it', 'Hitting hurts someone and makes the cross feeling bigger' and 'You can feel two things at once'. A star streak rewards runs of correct answers.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short, concrete sentences with everyday words (happy, cross, hug a teddy, tell a grown-up) and pass the family kid FK 5.0 limit. The lab uses one-line events a 5-year-old can picture, labels every face with its word, and has a large fixed set of five feelings. The adult text stays under FK 10 and ends with a concrete bedtime feelings-line routine.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid paragraph does one job: feelings change in a day, big feelings pass, the same thing gives different feelings, and nobody's feeling is wrong. The adult paragraphs give the three ideas with curriculum links, the reason feelings differ, named mistakes, and a home routine. Each of the six lab steps works on a different idea; none repeats another.

mobile.evidence: I checked iPhone 13 (390 px) screenshots in dark and light themes for every step. The event card, mood line, time labels, clue boxes, helper cards and reply bubbles all fit without clipping, and long replies wrap to two lines. The face chips have a radius of about 28-32 px with a 6 px hit margin, the young class gives 56 px buttons, and dragging faces and helper cards works with touch.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a labelled button twin: five feeling buttons (named for the current child in the two-child step), Next thing, six helper buttons, the three replies and Start again. The canvas aria-label is rewritten after every action with the event, the feeling chosen and why it fits or not. The challenge uses a polite live region, and the walkthrough's axe scan was clean in both themes on desktop and phone. Feelings are always named in words as well as shown by colour.
